title: Phase 5: Sell the beta on the customer's own AWS
description:
Outcome: chattic.us converts strangers into paying beta customers on a **ladder of delegated responsibility**, from forking the MIT-licensed code and running it yourself, through a $20 a month managed service in your own AWS account, to Anthus professional services adapting a deployment to your exact needs. A CTA on the marketing home page leads to a pitch page that states every cost up front, gated by a survey that qualifies the lead and prices the product.

Not included: AWS Marketplace listing, reseller billing (Path B is delivered by hand), a second sign-in provider, per-seat pricing.

## The three things this initiative rests on

**1. Chatticus already has a waitlist.** docs/ORGANIZATIONS.md: "Google sign-in is the waitlist form; POST /organizations creates a pending org." Organizations land pending, an operator enables them through the members CLI, and routing is already default-deny for waitlisted principals. Nothing here builds a second waitlist. It puts a survey and a payment in front of that transition and adds the step bring-your-own-AWS forces: provisioning.

**2. The pitch is control plus access, not features.** Control is the architecture: your AWS account, your data, MIT-licensed code you can fork. Access is what a closed product cannot offer — the people who wrote it run their own business on it, and the managed service puts you next to them. Each half fixes the other weakness. Control alone is a self-hosting chore; access alone is every other vendor.

**3. Self-setup is the default, and its template quality is the business model.** If a competent person with an AWS account can run the template unaided, most customers take the free setup path, margins hold, and engineer hours go to services work worth selling. If they cannot, everyone falls back to the $100 assisted path, Anthus loses money on each one, and the hours meant for services get spent on setup instead.

## Prices

| Item | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| Managed operation | $20 / month |
| Self-setup | $0 |
| Assisted setup | $100 once |
| AWS infrastructure | billed to the customer |
| Model tokens | billed to the customer |
| Professional services | quoted |

Round numbers on purpose. $19.95 undercuts a page whose argument is that we are being straight about cost. The monthly price is a deliberately floated research instrument; the other rows are not, and all of them are stated together or the research measures the wrong number.

## How to work this initiative

Every child carries a header naming its phase, what blocks it, what it runs in parallel with, and what it unblocks. **Phases run in sequence. Everything inside a phase runs at the same time.** Filter by the phase-N label.

| Phase | Epic | Items |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **935a98** Delegation ladder on the site | 4f9b03, 100b12, fb60d6, then 319834, bc8437, b4f849 |
| 1 | **b95aac** Beta pitch and waitlist survey | c7c7c1, then 0112aa, 98b4d9, 9ae395, e8f75f, 500adf; 47892b, 6525a7, 58d81d |
| 1 | **598be4** Cross-account provisioning | b88c0a, 8a25af, then 036750, 812b47, 9f5001, then 061a11; f90c39 |
| 2 | **b2de88** Waitlist triage and the operator queue | de3a66, 4e14ec, then 49324d, then 786185, 36fc27 |
| 3 | **e26358** Paid enablement through Stripe | 8f0780, 54f1cf, then ca62f9, cc6d0a, then 7370ef, ab10be |
| 4 | **5b2131** Managed updates into customer accounts | b47c1b, 0b43a4, then 2adb06, 911a49, 29387f |
| 4 | **ca57c7** Spend visibility and ceilings | 43e64c, then 39d8f5, 6a9e97, 9563cb |
| 5 | **29f5b5** Market research readout | 4b8c82 first; 9d8cde, 9860a5, 1aef04, then ae4414, 903bc9, 399c54 |

**Critical path:** c7c7c1 to 0112aa to 9ae395 to de3a66 to 49324d to 786185 to ca62f9 to 7370ef. The provisioning track (b88c0a to 8a25af to 036750 to 061a11) runs beside it and joins at 7370ef.

**Four items that gate more than their size suggests.**

- **b88c0a** — one throwaway AWS account provisioned by hand, timed. The setup fee, the invitation rate, and the onboarding promise all currently rest on a number nobody has measured. Publishing a CTA first commits the company to a service it has never performed.
- **036750** — self-setup working unaided. Rest of the business model, per point 3 above.
- **4f9b03** — what managed operation actually includes. The ladder section and the beta page both quote it and neither can be written honestly until it exists.
- **6525a7** — every cost stated above the first survey question, with a guard. It will look like copy. Copy gets edited by whoever is closest to the page, and the moment $20 appears without the AWS bill beside it the price research is measuring the wrong number.

**Serialize-merge hazard.** 061a11 moves where compute launches — computer_start, the worker credentials seam, the computer stack. Clear window, merged alone.

## Rules for every item

- Gherkin first. Scenarios fail for the right reason before production code exists.
- Reuse pending/enabled/suspended. Stripe becomes a second caller of the enable path the members CLI already calls. No parallel subscription status.
- Anthus organizations take every release before any customer does, and the rollout refuses to advance until they have. That order is the marketing claim and the release gate at once.
- Never touch an unmanaged deployment. An update applied to an organization that did not buy management is an unauthorized change in someone else AWS account.
- AWS resources are CDK only. The customer-facing cross-account template is versioned in the repository and a change to it is customer-visible.
- Never ask a customer for AdministratorAccess. Scoped role, per-organization ExternalId, published policy.
- Secrets never enter the repository, a CDK template, or an agent transcript.

comments.text:
As a team going to market, I want strangers to arrive from the marketing site, tell us who they are and what they need, pay us, and end up running Chatticus in their own AWS account, so that we learn what this is worth while every onboarding puts an Anthus engineer in the room with a decision-maker.

Definition of done: a CTA on the chattic.us home page leads to a pitch page stating all four costs; a survey gate qualifies and prices; scored signups are invited by an operator; Stripe collects a setup fee and a trialing subscription; a paid organization is provisioned into the customer's own AWS account and enabled; and the beta ends with a defensible answer on price, on whether the audience can even run on AWS, and on which sign-in provider to add next.

comments.text:
Design reasoning, the full nineteen-question survey, the scoring table, the two AWS setup paths, and the rejected alternatives are written up here: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/9ad7059f-4be8-4fec-bdc9-41b1f8a1777b

Three decisions recorded there that the child issues assume rather than re-argue:

1. **No authentication on the survey, and no GitHub sign-in.** Auth appears once, at checkout. GitHub is deferred because the identity kernel is keyed on verified email and GitHub routinely returns a private or unverified one. Revisited in 399c54, from survey evidence.
2. **AWS Resource Access Manager is not the deployment mechanism.** It shares specific resources across accounts and is right for placing the computer inside a VPC the customer already owns. Deploying into their account is a cross-account IAM role with a per-organization ExternalId, run from a CloudFormation template we publish.
3. **Path A ships, Path B is delivered by hand.** An account Anthus creates and re-bills makes us an AWS reseller with credit risk and a partner-status question. That is a real business, not one to acquire by accident during a beta. AWS Marketplace is the eventual answer to the billing question and should not be foreclosed by the role design.

comments.text:
Pricing and positioning revised after review. Superseding the earlier version of this description:

- **$20 and $100, round numbers.** Was $19.95. A page arguing that it states every cost up front should not price like a supermarket shelf.
- **The setup fee is structural, not promotional.** Waived by self-setup, charged for an assisted session. This is what stops the beta spending every engineer hour on $20 accounts, and it creates a genuine self-serve rung that the first version of this plan did not have.
- **The offer is a ladder, four rungs**, from forking the MIT-licensed code to professional services. Two new epics: 935a98 puts the ladder on the marketing site, 5b2131 builds the managed updates that are what the $20 actually buys.
- **The pitch is control plus access.** Control is architectural and already half-said on the site. Access is proximity to a team dogfooding an agent farm at the front of the field — which a closed product cannot offer at any price, and which is available at this level only because the beta is small. Say that out loud.

Note for whoever prices the assisted path: **$100 does not cover an engineer session at fully loaded cost.** It is a deliberate subsidy justified by the services conversation it creates, which is also why it has to stay the exception rather than the default.
